4.1Proton transfer equilibria in water (Brønsted acidity)

Decision flow
  1. Does the species donate or accept H⁺?
  2. Donates → Brønsted acid (proton donor) / accepts → Brønsted base (proton acceptor)
  3. Acid minus H⁺ = conjugate base; base plus H⁺ = conjugate acid
  4. Compare strengths → use $K_\text{a}$ (or p$K_\text{a}$): larger $K_\text{a}$ (smaller p$K_\text{a}$) = stronger acid

In the Brønsted–Lowry definition (1923), the essential feature of an acid–base reaction is the transfer of H⁺ (a proton). It applies in any solvent, or with no solvent at all.

A substance such as water that can act as both an acid and a base is amphiprotic. H⁺ never exists alone in water; it is written simply as the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺ (in reality it forms hydrogen-bonded clusters such as H₉O₄⁺).

(a) Conjugate acids and bases

General form: $\text{Acid}_1 + \text{Base}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Acid}_2 + \text{Base}_1$. Example: the conjugate base of HF is F⁻; the conjugate acid of NH₃ is NH₄⁺.

(b) Strengths of acids and bases: acidity and basicity constants

Acidity constant: $K_\text{a} = [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{X}^-]/[\text{HX}]$ (activity of water taken as 1). If $K_\text{a} \ll 1$, the acid is mostly un-ionized in solution.

Basicity constant: $K_\text{b} = [\text{HB}^+][\text{OH}^-]/[\text{B}]$. Autoprotolysis constant of water: $K_\text{w} = [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{OH}^-] = 1.00\times10^{-14}$ (25°C).

For a conjugate pair: $K_\text{a}K_\text{b} = K_\text{w}$, i.e. p$K_\text{a}$ + p$K_\text{b}$ = p$K_\text{w}$ = 14.00. → The stronger the base, the weaker its conjugate acid. Base strength is conventionally reported as the p$K_\text{a}$ of the conjugate acid.

(c) Strong and weak acids

  • Strong acid: p$K_\text{a}$ < 0 (essentially fully deprotonated in water), e.g. HCl
  • Weak acid: p$K_\text{a}$ > 0 (much un-ionized HA remains), e.g. HF, H₂CO₃
  • Strong base: almost fully protonated in water (e.g. O²⁻ → OH⁻ immediately). The conjugate base of a strong acid is a weak base.

(d) Polyprotic acids

Protons are lost in succession, and usually $K_\text{a1} > K_\text{a2} > \cdots$ (it is harder to pull H⁺ away from an ion with more negative charge). Example: H₂S p$K_\text{a1}$ = 7.04, p$K_\text{a2}$ ≈ 19.

Distribution diagram: fraction $f$ of each species plotted against pH. At pH = p$K_\text{a}$ the fractions of the two neighbouring species are equal.

(e) Factors governing Brønsted acid and base strength

Gas-phase proton affinity $A_\text{p}$ = the negative of the enthalpy of the gas-phase proton-gain reaction $\text{A}^-(\text{g}) + \text{H}^+(\text{g}) \to \text{HA}(\text{g})$ ($A_\text{p} = -\Delta_\text{pg}H^\ominus$).

Thermodynamic cycle: $A_\text{p}(\text{A}^-) = B(\text{H–A}) + I(\text{H}) - A_\text{e}(\text{A})$. For p-block conjugate bases, $A_\text{p}$ decreases to the right along a period and down a group → HI is the strongest acid, CH₄ the weakest (mainly rising electron affinity and falling H–A bond energy).

Solvation: Born equation $\Delta_\text{solv}G^\ominus = -\dfrac{N_\text{A}z^2e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_\text{r}}\right)$ → ions with high charge and small radius are stabilized most. Electrostatic parameter $\xi = 100z^2/(r/\text{pm})$.

A polar solvent stabilizes the anion A⁻ → the acidity of a neutral acid HA increases. Cationic acids (NH₄⁺ etc.) are stabilized by solvation, so their acidity decreases. F⁻, OH⁻ and Cl⁻ are stabilized more than the Born equation predicts because of hydrogen bonding.

4.2Periodic trends in aqua acid strength

Decision flow
  1. Where is the acidic proton?
  2. On H₂O coordinated to a central metal → aqua acid (e.g. [Fe(OH₂)₆]³⁺)
  3. On –OH with no neighbouring =O → hydroxoacid (e.g. Te(OH)₆)
  4. On –OH with =O on the same atom → oxoacid (e.g. H₂SO₄ = O₂S(OH)₂)

The three classes can be seen as successive deprotonation stages: aqua acid →(−H⁺)→ hydroxoacid →(−H⁺)→ oxoacid. Seen for d-block metals in intermediate oxidation states (e.g. Ru(IV)).

Aqua acids are typical of central atoms in low oxidation states (s- and d-block metals); oxoacids of central atoms in high oxidation states (right of the p block, etc.).

Aqua acid strength

Decision flow
  1. Check the charge $z$ and radius $r$ of the central metal ion
  2. Large $z$, small $r$ (large $\xi$) → stronger aqua acid (smaller p$K_\text{a}$)
  3. Off the line? → covalent character of the M–O bond (Hg²⁺, Sn²⁺, Cu²⁺ are more acidic than predicted)

Ionic model: the positive charge repels the proton. Most Group 1 and 2 aqua ions are very weak acids (essentially neutral).

4.3Simple oxoacids

Mononuclear oxoacids: H₂CO₃, HNO₃, H₃PO₄, H₂SO₄ etc. Oxoacids are formed by electronegative elements at the upper right of the periodic table.

(a) Substituted oxoacids

Replace –OH with another group: a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent (e.g. F) makes the acid stronger (O₂SF(OH) is stronger than H₂SO₄). A π-donating group such as –NH₂ makes it weaker.

Trap: an H bonded directly to the central atom is not acidic. Phosphonic acid H₃PO₃ = OPH(OH)₂ is only diprotic.

(b) Pauling's rules

Decision flow
  1. Write the formula as O$_p$E(OH)$_q$ and count the nonprotonated O atoms $p$
  2. Rule 1: p$K_\text{a}$ ≈ $8 - 5p$ ($p$=0 → 8, 1 → 3, 2 → −2, 3 → −7)
  3. Rule 2: successive p$K_\text{a}$ values of a polyprotic acid ($q>1$) increase by 5 units

Reason: more =O groups let the negative charge of the conjugate base be delocalized by resonance over more O atoms, stabilizing it.

Example: acid strength HClO₄ > HClO₃ > HClO₂ > HClO. H₂SO₄ ($p$=2) is predicted to have p$K_\text{a1}$ ≈ −2 and p$K_\text{a2}$ ≈ 3.

(c) Structural anomalies

H₂CO₃: Pauling predicts p$K_\text{a1}$ ≈ 3 but the measured value is 6.4, because only about 1% of dissolved CO₂ is present as H₂CO₃. Corrected, the true p$K_\text{a1}$ ≈ 3.6.

H₂SO₃ has not been detected as a molecule in solution; it is really dissolved SO₂ (SO₂·nH₂O). HSO₃⁻ also has tautomers.

4.4Anhydrous oxides

Decision flow
  1. Is the oxide-forming element a metal or a nonmetal?
  2. Nonmetal → acidic oxide: gives an acid with water / reacts with bases (e.g. CO₂ + H₂O → OC(OH)₂)
  3. Metal → basic oxide: gives a base with water / reacts with acids (e.g. BaO + H₂O → Ba(OH)₂)
  4. Near the metal–nonmetal frontier → amphoteric oxide: reacts with both acids and bases

(a) Acidic and basic oxides

An acidic oxide acts as a Lewis acid, accepting OH⁻: $\text{CO}_2 + \text{OH}^- \to \text{O}_2\text{C(OH)}^-$. The O²⁻ of a basic oxide acts as a Lewis/Brønsted base: $\text{BaO} + 2\text{H}_3\text{O}^+ \to \text{Ba}^{2+} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

(b) Amphoterism

Example: Al₂O₃ dissolves in both acid and base ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2[\text{Al(OH}_2)_6]^{3+}$ / $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{OH}^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2[\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$).

Amphoterism is found for the light elements of Groups 2 and 13 (BeO, Al₂O₃, Ga₂O₃), the d block (TiO₂, V₂O₅) and heavier p-block elements (SnO₂, Sb₂O₅).

In the d block, higher oxidation numbers give more acidic oxides and lower ones more basic oxides. Highest-oxidation-state oxides (Mn₂O₇ etc.) are acidic.

Qualitative analysis: Al(III) and Cr(III) are amphoteric and redissolve in excess NaOH (aluminate/chromate ions) → separation from other hydroxides.

4.5Polyoxo compound formation

Decision flow
  1. Acids and aqua ions containing –OH condense (H₂O is lost)
  2. Oxoanions → lowering the pH (acidifying) forms polyoxoanions
  3. Aqua cations → raising the pH forms polycations → eventually a hydroxide precipitate

Example: condensation of phosphate $2\text{PO}_4^{3-} + 2\text{H}_3\text{O}^+ \to \text{P}_2\text{O}_7^{4-} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (diphosphate ion).

In biology: ATP hydrolysis $\text{ATP}^{4-} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{ADP}^{3-} + \text{HPO}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, $\Delta_\text{r}G^\ominus$ = −41 kJ mol⁻¹ (pH 7.4) supplies energy. The P–O–P link is thermodynamically unstable but kinetically stable.

Polyoxoanions make up most of the oxygen in the Earth's crust (silicate minerals). Example: MgSiO₃ contains infinite SiO₃²⁻ chains.

d-block elements in high oxidation states — V(V), Mo(VI), W(VI) (and Nb(V), Ta(V), Cr(VI)) — form polyoxometalates.

4.6Examples of Lewis acids and bases

Decision flow
  1. Species that accepts an electron pair → Lewis acid (A) / species that donates one → Lewis base (:B)
  2. Basic reaction: A + :B → A–B (complex/adduct), forming a coordinate (dative) bond

MO view: the Lewis acid provides its LUMO (empty orbital), the Lewis base its HOMO (lone-pair orbital); 2 electrons enter the new bonding orbital → energy is lowered.

Terminology: in thermodynamic (equilibrium) contexts we say acid/base; in kinetic contexts an electron-pair donor is a nucleophile and an acceptor an electrophile.

H⁺ is a Lewis acid → every Brønsted acid "exhibits" Lewis acidity (HA is a complex of H⁺ and A⁻). Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base. The Lewis definition extends to systems with no protons.

Species that can act as Lewis acids

  • Molecules with an incomplete octet, e.g. B(CH₃)₃ + :NH₃ → adduct
  • Metal cations, e.g. Co²⁺ forms [Co(OH₂)₆]²⁺ with H₂O
  • Molecules with a full octet that can rearrange to accept a pair, e.g. CO₂ + OH⁻ → HCO₃⁻
  • Molecules that can expand their valence shell, e.g. SiF₄ + 2F⁻ → [SiF₆]²⁻ (halides of heavier p-block elements)

4.7Group characteristics of Lewis acids

Decision flow
  1. Which group is the compound from?
  2. Group 1 (alkali metal ions) → Lewis complexes with water (hydrated ions)
  3. Group 13 BX₃ → empty p orbital is the acceptor. Lewis acidity BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃
  4. Group 14 (not C) → become 5- or 6-coordinate by hypervalence
  5. Group 15 → oxides and halides of the heavier elements (SbF₅ etc.)
  6. Group 16 → SO₂ (accepts at S), SO₃ (strong Lewis acid)
  7. Group 17 → Br₂, I₂ are mild Lewis acids

(a) s-block elements

Alkali metal ions form Lewis complexes with water molecules (hydration). BeCl₂ adopts a Cl-bridged chain structure in the solid.

(b) Group 13

BX₃ is trigonal planar with an empty p orbital → forms adducts with amines etc. and becomes pyramidal.

Electronegativity alone would make BF₃ the strongest, but the real order is BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃ because p–p π bonding is strongest between B and the small F atom, and this π bond is lost on complex formation.

Aluminium halides are dimers in the gas phase (Al₂Cl₆). AlCl₃ catalyses Friedel–Crafts reactions (abstracts Cl⁻ from RCl to give R⁺).

(c) Group 14

Si, Ge, Sn and Pb can become 5- or 6-coordinate: $\text{SiF}_4 + 2\text{F}^- \to [\text{SiF}_6]^{2-}$. Lewis acidity: SiF₄ > SiCl₄ > SiBr₄ > SiI₄ (more electron-withdrawing F → stronger).

SnCl₂ is both a Lewis acid and a Lewis base: it forms [SnCl₃]⁻ with Cl⁻, and [SnCl₃]⁻ uses its lone pair to coordinate to a metal (Mn). Sn(IV) halide strength: SnF₄ > SnCl₄ > SnBr₄ > SnI₄.

(d) Group 15

SbF₅ is a powerful Lewis acid: $\text{SbF}_5 + 2\text{HF} \to \text{H}_2\text{F}^+ + [\text{SbF}_6]^-$ → used to make superacids.

(e) Group 16

SO₂ can be a Lewis acid (accepting at S) or a Lewis base (donating a lone pair from S or O). SO₃ is a strong Lewis acid (and a weak O-donor base).

Sulfuric acid manufacture: SO₃ is absorbed not in water but in H₂SO₄ to give H₂S₂O₇ (oleum), which is then hydrolysed (to control the heat released).

(f) Group 17

Br₂ and I₂ are mild Lewis acids that accept a pair into their σ* orbital (LUMO). Their complexes are coloured by charge-transfer transitions (I₂ is violet to brown depending on solvent). Example: $\text{I}_2 + \text{I}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{I}_3^-$ ($K$ = 725).

4.8The fundamental types of reaction

Decision flow
  1. What happened between reactants and products?
  2. Free A and free :B combine → complex formation: A + :B → A–B
  3. An acid/base in a complex is driven out by another → displacement: B–A + :B′ → A–B′ + :B
  4. Partners are exchanged → metathesis: A–B + A′–B′ → A–B′ + A′–B

(a) Complex formation

Both reactants exist independently and form a complex by HOMO–LUMO interaction. Examples: $\text{F}_3\text{B} + :\text{NH}_3 \to \text{F}_3\text{B–NH}_3$, SO₃ + :OMe₂.

(b) Displacement reactions

Example: Et₂O–BF₃ + pyridine → py–BF₃ + Et₂O. Every Brønsted proton-transfer reaction (HS⁻ + H₂O → H₂S + OH⁻) is a kind of displacement.

(c) Metathesis reactions

Displacement assisted by abstraction of the base by another acid. Example: Me₃SiI + AgBr → Me₃SiBr + AgI (driven by formation of the less soluble AgI).

4.9Hard and soft acids and bases (HSAB)

Decision flow
  1. What is the order of complex stability with the halide ions?
  2. I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ → hard acid (class a)
  3. F⁻ < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻ → soft acid (class b)
  4. Rule: hard acids bind preferentially to hard bases, soft acids to soft bases

For Hg²⁺, $K_\text{f}$ rises steeply from F⁻ to I⁻ → soft acid. Pb²⁺ follows the same direction gently → borderline soft. Zn²⁺ goes the other way → borderline hard. Al³⁺ falls steeply → hard acid.

Rule of thumb: small, weakly polarizable cations are hard; large, highly polarizable cations are soft. Also for neutral molecules: phenol binds (C₂H₅)₂O strongly → hard; I₂ binds (C₂H₅)₂S strongly → soft.

ClassAcidsBases
HardH⁺, Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Be²⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺, Cr³⁺, Fe³⁺, BF₃, SO₃F⁻, OH⁻, H₂O, NH₃, CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻, O²⁻, SO₄²⁻, PO₄³⁻, ClO₄⁻
BorderlineFe²⁺, Co²⁺, Ni²⁺, Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺, Pb²⁺, SO₂, BBr₃NO₂⁻, SO₃²⁻, Br⁻, N₃⁻, N₂, C₅H₅N, SCN⁻ (N-bound)
SoftCu⁺, Ag⁺, Au⁺, Tl⁺, Hg₂²⁺, Pd²⁺, Cd²⁺, Pt²⁺, Hg²⁺, BH₃H⁻, R⁻, CN⁻, CO, I⁻, SCN⁻ (S-bound), R₃P, C₆H₆, R₂S

(b) Interpretation of hardness

Hard–hard interactions are mainly electrostatic (ionic); soft–soft interactions are mainly covalent.

Example: $\text{BeI}_2 + \text{HgF}_2 \to \text{BeF}_2 + \text{HgI}_2$ is exothermic because Be–F (632 kJ/mol) is a strong hard–hard bond.

(c) Chemical consequences of hardness

Geochemistry: hard cations (Li⁺, Mg²⁺, Ti⁴⁺, Cr³⁺) bind O²⁻ and occur in silicates as lithophiles. Soft cations (Cd²⁺, Pb²⁺, Sb³⁺, Bi³⁺) bind S²⁻ etc. and occur in sulfide minerals as chalcophiles.

Ambidentate SCN⁻: binds hard acids through the hard N and soft acids (e.g. Pt(II)) through the soft S.

(d) Other contributions to complex formation

  • Competition with the solvent (the solvent is itself a Lewis acid/base)
  • Rearrangement of substituents of the acid or base (cost of structural change)
  • Steric hindrance: an acid–base pair too bulky to form a complex = a frustrated Lewis pair (can split H₂ heterolytically to activate it)

4.10Thermodynamic acidity parameters (Drago–Wayland equation)

Decision flow
  1. Want to estimate the standard enthalpy of complex formation
  2. Read $E_\text{A}, C_\text{A}$ of the acid and $E_\text{B}, C_\text{B}$ of the base from the table
  3. $-\Delta_\text{f}H^\ominus(\text{A–B})/(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}) = E_\text{A}E_\text{B} + C_\text{A}C_\text{B}$

$E$ represents the electrostatic (ionic) contribution and $C$ the covalent contribution. Reproduces >1500 complexes to about ±3 kJ/mol.

Species$E$$C$
BF₃ (acid)20.23.31
I₂ (acid)2.052.05
Phenol (acid)8.860.90
Ammonia (base)2.787.08
Pyridine (base)2.3913.10
Dimethylsulfide (base)0.7015.26

Example: BF₃ + NH₃: $-\Delta H = 20.2\times2.78 + 3.31\times7.08 =$ ≈ 79.6 kJ mol⁻¹.

Limitation: only applies to reactions in the gas phase or in noncoordinating nonpolar solvents (in water the solvent competes).

4.11Solvent levelling

Decision flow
  1. Acid HA in solvent HSol: p$K_\text{a}$ < 0?
  2. Yes → HA is levelled all the way to H₂Sol⁺ (cannot be distinguished)
  3. Base in solvent: p$K_\text{a}$ (conjugate acid) > p$K_\text{sol}$ → levelled to Sol⁻
  4. Window of distinguishable strengths = p$K_\text{a}$ 0 to p$K_\text{sol}$ (width ∝ autoprotolysis constant)

In water the strongest acid is H₃O⁺ and the strongest base OH⁻. HBr and HI look equally strong in water → distinguish them in a less basic solvent such as ethanoic acid.

Water: p$K_\text{w}$ = 14; liquid ammonia: p$K_\text{am}$ = 33; DMSO: p$K_\text{auto}$ = 37 (a wide window).

To study base strengths, a more acidic solvent helps (a strong base such as NH₂⁻ is levelled to OH⁻ in water).

4.12The solvent-system definition of acids and bases

Decision flow
  1. Identify the cation and anion from the solvent's autoionization
  2. Solute increases the concentration of the solvent's cation → acid
  3. Solute increases the concentration of the solvent's anion → base

Extends Brønsted–Lowry to aprotic solvents where no protons are transferred.

Example: $2\text{BrF}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{BrF}_2^+ + \text{BrF}_4^-$. SbF₅ is an acid in BrF₃ (increases BrF₂⁺: $\text{SbF}_5 + \text{BrF}_3 \to \text{BrF}_2^+ + \text{SbF}_6^-$); KF is a base (increases BrF₄⁻).

4.13Solvents as acids and bases

Decision flow
  1. What kind of solvent?
  2. Basic solvent (DMSO, DMF, pyridine…) → complexes the solute and takes part in displacement reactions
  3. Acidic solvent (HF, H₂SO₄) → readily protonates bases
  4. Aprotic but autoionizing (N₂O₄, BrF₃) → treat with the solvent-system definition

(a) Basic solvents

Example: DMSO has both a hard O and a soft S donor (ambidentate). The solvent can be displaced, as in $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{SO–SO}_2 + \text{NH}_3$.

(b) Acidic and neutral solvents

Hydrogen bonding is also an example of Lewis complex formation: A–H···:B. SO₂ is a good solvent for soft bases (benzene etc.).

(c) Liquid ammonia

B.p. −33°C. $2\text{NH}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{NH}_2^-$ (p$K_\text{am}$ = 33). Acids increase NH₄⁺, bases increase NH₂⁻. Many reactions parallel those in water: $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NaNH}_2 \to \text{NaCl} + 2\text{NH}_3$.

Alkali metals dissolve to give solvated electrons and blue conducting solutions: $\text{Na} \to \text{Na}^+ + \text{e}^-(\text{am})$.

(d) Hydrogen fluoride

Liquid HF: strongly acidic, high relative permittivity (ε_r = 84 at 0°C). $3\text{HF} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2\text{F}^+ + \text{HF}_2^-$. The conjugate base F⁻ hydrogen-bonds to HF to give HF₂⁻. It attacks glass.

(e) Anhydrous sulfuric acid

High relative permittivity and viscosity (strong hydrogen bonding). $2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{SO}_4^+ + \text{HSO}_4^-$ plus several side reactions. HNO₃ acts as a base in H₂SO₄, generating the nitronium ion NO₂⁺ (aromatic nitration).

(f) Dinitrogen tetroxide

Two autoionizations: $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{NO}^+ + \text{NO}_3^-$ and $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{NO}_2^-$. Adding an electron-pair donor (Et₂O etc.) favours the NO⁺ route; an acceptor such as BF₃ favours the NO₂⁺ route.

(g) Ionic liquids

Salts melting below 100°C (asymmetric quaternary ammonium cations + AlCl₄⁻ etc.). Polar, nonvolatile, wide electrochemical window → solvents that can hold very high concentrations of Lewis acid/base catalysts.

(h) Supercritical fluids

Above the critical point the liquid and vapour phases become indistinguishable. scCO₂: $P_\text{c}$ = 72.8 atm, $T_\text{c}$ = 30.95°C. CO₂ can be a Lewis base (through O) or a Lewis acid (at C).

Uses: decaffeinating coffee, replacing organic solvents (removed and recycled by depressurizing; nonflammable). Supercritical water ($T_\text{c}$ = 374°C, $P_\text{c}$ = 218 atm) dissolves organics but is a poor solvent for ions.

4.14Superacids and superbases

Decision flow
  1. More efficient proton donor than anhydrous sulfuric acid? → superacid
  2. More efficient proton acceptor than OH⁻? → superbase

Superacids are made by dissolving a powerful Lewis acid (SbF₅ etc.) in a Brønsted acid (HF, HSO₃F): $\text{SbF}_5 + 2\text{HSO}_3\text{F} \to [\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3\text{F}]^+ + [\text{SbF}_5(\text{SO}_3\text{F})]^-$. SbF₅/HSO₃F is "magic acid".

Use of superacids: unstable cations such as carbocations can be observed as stable species (Olah, Nobel Prize 1994).

Examples of superbases: hydride and nitride ions (NaH, Li₃N, LiNH₂ etc.). $\text{Li}_3\text{N} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 3\text{LiOH} + \text{NH}_3$. Hydride H⁻ reacts with water to release H₂.

4.15Heterogeneous acid–base reactions

Decision flow
  1. What acid sites are on the solid surface?
  2. Surface –OH → Brønsted acid sites
  3. Coordinatively unsaturated metal (Al³⁺ etc.) → Lewis acid sites

Example: Si–OH groups on silica gel act as Brønsted sites for surface-modification reactions (chromatographic stationary phases etc.). Aluminosilicates (zeolites) are important petrochemical catalysts.

With benzyl chloride, Lewis acid sites are involved; with benzyl alcohol, Brønsted acid sites are involved.

KCKey concepts summary

  • Brønsted: transfer of H⁺. $K_\text{a}K_\text{b}$ = $K_\text{w}$; p$K_\text{a}$ < 0 = strong acid.
  • Gas-phase proton affinity $A_\text{p}$ falls to the right and down a group → HI is the strongest hydrohalic acid.
  • Aqua acids: stronger for large $z$, small $r$ (large $\xi$); more acidic than predicted when M–O is covalent.
  • Pauling: p$K_\text{a}$ ≈ $8-5p$; successive p$K_\text{a}$ rise by 5. Beware the "anomalies" of H₂CO₃ and H₃PO₃.
  • Oxides: metal → basic, nonmetal → acidic, frontier → amphoteric. Higher oxidation number → more acidic.
  • Lewis: electron-pair acceptor/donor (LUMO–HOMO). Reactions: complex formation, displacement, metathesis.
  • BX₃ Lewis acidity: BF₃ < BCl₃ < BBr₃ (loss of π bonding).
  • HSAB: hard–hard = electrostatic, soft–soft = covalent. Drago–Wayland: $-\Delta H = E_\text{A}E_\text{B}+C_\text{A}C_\text{B}$.
  • Levelling: the distinguishable range in a solvent is p$K_\text{a}$ = 0 to p$K_\text{sol}$.
